title: How would you estimate the yearly revenue of all car washes in the US?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "What is the yearly revenue of all car washes in the US?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: US car washes take roughly $13 billion a year: about $8.6B from pay-per-wash customers and $4.2B from unlimited-wash memberships. Splitting those two ways of paying is the key step, because a member who washes three times a month pays a flat fee, not three wash prices. Have a go yourself before reading on.
body:
The question

What is the yearly revenue of all car washes in the US?

Clarify what counts as a car wash:

  • In: automatic tunnels, in-bay automatics at gas stations, self-serve bays and hand-wash sites.
  • Out: washing at home, and full detailing (interior valeting, paint correction), which is a different service at a different price.
  • Vehicles: cars, SUVs and pick-ups. Heavy trucks and buses use specialist washes; leave them out.
"I'll size consumer car wash revenue for light vehicles, excluding detailing and fleet truck washes."

The approach: vehicles × how they pay

The one-line version is vehicles × paid washes per year × average price. With 290M vehicles, 3 washes and $15, that gives about $13.1B. It is a reasonable start, but it hides the biggest change in the industry: unlimited-wash memberships. A member pays a monthly fee however often they visit, so multiplying their visits by a single wash price overstates revenue.

So split vehicles into three groups:

  1. Members on a monthly plan: members × monthly fee × 12.
  2. Pay-per-wash users: vehicles × washes a year × price per wash.
  3. Non-users: people who wash at home or not at all. Zero revenue.

Step by step

Start with 280M light vehicles. The Federal Highway Administration counted 298M registered motor vehicles in 2024, but that includes heavy trucks, buses and motorcycles, so about 280M cars, SUVs and pick-ups is a sensible round number.

SegmentShareVehiclesSpend each a yearRevenue
Members5%14M$25 × 12 = $300$4.2B
Pay-per-wash55%154M4 washes × $14 = $56$8.6B
Non-users40%112M$0$0
Total100%280M$12.8B

Answer: about $13B a year. Members are only 5% of vehicles but a third of revenue ($4.2B of $12.8B), which explains why operators push memberships so hard: predictable monthly income and loyal customers.

Sanity check from a second angle

Per vehicle. $12.8B ÷ 280M is about $46 per vehicle a year, roughly three or four washes. For the average car, washed professionally every few months, that sounds right.

From the supply side. Assume one car wash of some kind for every 6,000 people. With about 335M people, that is about 56,000 sites. $12.8B ÷ 56,000 = about $230,000 per site a year, or about $630 a day. At $14 a wash, that is roughly 45 cars a day on average. A busy tunnel does far more and a single self-serve bay far fewer, so an average of a few dozen cars a day across all formats is plausible.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I estimate about $13 billion a year. Roughly $8.6 billion comes from 154 million vehicles washed four times a year at $14, and $4.2 billion from 14 million members paying $25 a month. Members are a third of revenue from 5% of cars, so membership share is the number I'd want to test. As a check, it works out at about 45 washes a day per site across 56,000 sites, which seems reasonable."

A weak answer multiplies every visit by one price, including members who wash ten times a month on a flat fee, and gets a much bigger number than the cash that actually changes hands.

Common mistakes

  • Visits × price for members. A member washing three times a month on a $25 plan pays about $8.33 a wash, not $14. Treat subscriptions as subscribers × fee × 12.
  • Counting every registered vehicle. Heavy trucks and motorcycles barely use consumer car washes.
  • Forgetting non-users. Plenty of people wash at home or not at all. Assuming every car uses a paid wash inflates the answer.
  • Mixing in detailing. It is a different service with prices many times higher. Keep it separate.

Practise it

1. Membership share doubles to 10%, all drawn from pay-per-wash users (who fall to 50%). What happens to revenue?

Show the answer

Members: 28M × $300 = $8.4B. Pay-per-wash: 140M × $56 = $7.84B. Total: about $16.2B, up from $12.8B. Each switcher goes from $56 a year to $300, so memberships grow the market as well as shifting it.

2. Members average three washes a month. If you had wrongly priced their visits at $14 each, what revenue would you have shown for members?

Show the answer

14M members × 36 washes × $14 = $7.1B, against the true $4.2B. You would have overstated member revenue by about $2.9B, or 68%.

3. A chain has 400 tunnel sites, each washing 300 cars a day for 360 days at an average of $10 a wash (after membership discounts). What is its revenue, and what share of the market?

Show the answer

400 × 300 × 360 × $10 = $432M a year. That is about 3.4% of a $12.8B market, which shows how fragmented the industry is even for a large chain.

Where to practise next

For another price-times-volume estimate in the US, try the US dog food market. Subscriptions change the maths in many industries; see unit economics explained and the three ways to set a price. The market sizing drills give you timed practice.
